title: The Diamond Sutra, first half
tomorrow: why would a sutra named for a diamond end with dew?

cards: The dishes are done and someone finally sits down, and that's exactly when the big question comes. That's how the Diamond Sutra opens. Morning near the city of Shravasti.
The Buddha puts on his robe, takes his bowl, walks into the city for alms, eats, comes back, puts the bowl away, washes his feet, and sits down. Nothing else happens.
Then an old monk named Subhuti stands up from the crowd, kneels, and asks: someone who sets out on the bodhisattva path, how should they stand, and how should they handle their mind?
And the answer that comes back sounds impossible.

teach.h: LEAD ALL BEINGS. NO BEING LED.
teach.b: Here it is, in paraphrase: lead every kind of being to nirvana, and know that no being has been led. Then, read the first half in one sitting, and a rhythm takes over.

Again and again, something is named, then cut, then named again: what is called a being is not a being; that's why it's called a being. On a slow read, one section at a time, that line can feel like a riddle.
In one sitting, it starts to feel like a blade going through every idea that tries to harden, even ideas about the Buddha, even ideas about this sutra.
The sutra says its own teaching is like a raft, to be left behind once you've crossed. That's why it's the diamond.
In the Sanskrit title, vajra is the diamond or thunderbolt, the thing nothing can cut that cuts everything else. A second thing jumps out in one sitting: a comparison that keeps coming back.

teach.h: FOUR LINES BEAT WORLDS OF TREASURE.
teach.b: Someone fills whole worlds with treasure and gives it all away; someone else keeps four lines of this teaching and explains them to others. The four lines win, every time.
And in the middle of the first half, Subhuti hears all this and weeps. So why open with lunch?
Perhaps because the diamond isn't kept for special moments. It cuts through ideas about bowls and feet and plain mornings too.

how: The Diamond Sutra is studied and recited in Mahayana traditions, especially in Chan and Zen; some practitioners read it straight through in one sitting as a practice.

o: a hymn praising the Buddha's crown and its jewels
a book of rules for monks who carry precious stones
a Mahayana text that cuts every fixed idea, like a gem

games.q: the first half, in one sitting — tap the pairs.
p: bowl, meal, washed feet, sitting down
asks how to stand and handle the mind
the teaching, left behind after crossing
outweigh worlds of treasure given away

s: the Diamond Sutra opens with a great miracle
it opens with the Buddha's alms round, his meal, washing his feet and sitting down.
the sutra calls its own teaching a raft to be left behind
once you've crossed, even the teaching isn't something to carry on your back.
in the first half, Subhuti is moved to tears

games.q: your friend says she's 'just not a creative person' and won't try the class. what would the diamond cut?
o: the fixed idea 'not creative': a label, not a fact about her.
the class itself: if she doesn't want it, no need to go.
her doubt, by proving she's secretly a born artist.
games.why: the sutra cuts every idea that tries to harden: being, self, even the Buddha. 'not a creative person' is one more idea.

practice: Find a bowl or a cup you ate or drank from today, or bring one to mind. Look at it the way the sutra's first scene looks at a bowl: used, washed, put away.
When a label comes, pretty, chipped, mine, notice the label, let it go, and look at the bowl again, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The Diamond Sutra: a Mahayana text in which the Buddha answers Subhuti's question by cutting through every fixed idea, like a diamond. Today, its first half, in one sitting.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the diamond (or thunderbolt) cutter, the sutra's title; vajra is what nothing can cut.

carryVoice: Your line: the diamond, cutting even the idea of itself. Half a sutra in one sitting, done.
